# Results — Study 416 (Rounding Bottom / saucer base)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a
rounding bottom (saucer base) marks accumulation, and the confirmed breakout above the rim
starts a sustained advance** — tested with the closest **mechanical** detector (a
least-squares parabola with positive curvature, a good fit, an interior trough, sufficient
depth, and a first close above the left-rim resistance). For each confirmed breakout we
enter the **next day's open** (one execution lag) and measure the forward 10 / 20 / 60-day
return against the **every-bar base rate** and a **date-shuffle placebo**. As-of
**2026-06-23**. Offline & deterministic once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to
reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted OHLC — SPY + 29 long-listed US large-caps (public, no key) |
| Window | 2004-01-02 → 2026-06-23 (**22.5** years; 5,653 bars/name) |
| Names | **30** (SPY + 29 large-caps) |
| Panel fingerprint | `69cb517da40d` |
| Detector | trailing window `base_len=90`; parabola $a>0$, $R^2\ge0.55$; vertex in central 60%; depth $\ge0.08$ (log) below rim; first close above the left-rim high; 30-bar cooldown |
| Timing / costs | enter **t+1 open**, exit close at t+1+H (one lag); 5 bps one-way × NAV round trip (long-only, no borrow) |

> **Survivorship (named on the Signal axis).** The basket is 30 names *still trading* in
> 2026. A surviving-names panel cannot include firms that delisted after a failed base, which
> mildly *flatters* any "the base works" finding — so a **null** result here is, if anything,
> a conservative (strong) null. Chart figures are also **partly subjective**: we test one
> reasonable mechanical definition and report robustness to its knobs (below).

## The signal — confirmed breakout vs the every-bar base rate

The decisive test is **not** the breakout return against zero (which only measures the equity
drift premium every long position earns) but against the **base rate** — the average forward
return of a *random day* in the same names. The placebo *p* is the share of 5,000 random-date
draws (matched to the per-name breakout count) whose pooled forward return **beats** the
observed breakout mean.

| horizon | n breakouts | gross | net (5 bps) | base rate | win% | base win% | one-sample *t* vs 0 | HAC *t* vs 0 | Welch *t* vs base | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 10-day | 184 | +0.53% | +0.43% | +0.59% | 51% | 57% | 1.42 | 1.22 | −0.15 | 0.569 |
| 20-day | 183 | +1.51% | +1.41% | +1.14% | 62% | 58% | **2.97** | **2.72** | 0.73 | 0.252 |
| 60-day | 181 | +4.07% | +3.97% | +3.31% | 65% | 63% | **4.52** | **4.42** | 0.84 | 0.205 |

Read it carefully. Against **zero**, the 20- and 60-day breakout returns clear the desk's
*t* ≥ 2 bar (t = 2.97, 4.52) — but that is the **equity drift premium**, not the figure:
a *random* day in the same stocks earns **+1.14% / +3.31%** over the same windows, almost
identical to the breakout's **+1.51% / +4.07%**. The honest **Welch *t* of breakout vs base
rate is only 0.73 / 0.84** — nowhere near 2 — and the **date-shuffle placebo** says random
entries beat the saucer ~20–25% of the time (p = 0.25 / 0.20). The saucer adds **nothing**
over just being long.

## Robustness — no detector knob rescues it

Chart figures are subjective, so the fair worry is "you drew the saucer wrong." Varying the
window length and the U-shape fit threshold leaves the verdict intact; the breakout-vs-base
*t* never clears 2, and the *stricter* (prettier) definitions go **negative**.

| variation | n breakouts | gross (20d) | one-sample *t* vs 0 | Welch *t* vs base | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| `base_len` = 60 | 235 | +1.12% | 2.50 | −0.05 | 0.542 |
| **`base_len` = 90** | **183** | **+1.51%** | **2.97** | **0.73** | **0.252** |
| `base_len` = 120 | 141 | +0.02% | 0.04 | **−1.80** | 0.969 |
| `R²_min` = 0.45 | 260 | +1.29% | 2.91 | 0.34 | 0.368 |
| `R²_min` = 0.70 | 59 | +0.87% | 1.20 | −0.37 | 0.603 |

The breakout-vs-base *t* ranges from **−1.80 to +0.73** across every configuration — never
significant, sometimes pointing the *wrong* way. A longer (more demanding) saucer actually
*underperforms* the base rate.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

On a deterministic panel we **plant the saucer shape**. With `edge = 0` the shape is present
but there is **no** post-breakout continuation — a true null the detector must NOT turn into
an edge. With `edge > 0` we plant a real drift the detector must recover.

| planted edge | n breakouts | gross (20d) | base rate | one-sample *t* vs 0 | Welch *t* vs base | placebo *p* | win% |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (shape only, no continuation) | 185 | +1.08% | +0.48% | 2.48 | 1.38 | 0.111 | 57% |
| **+0.10** (real planted drift) | 186 | +5.86% | +1.07% | 10.87 | **8.87** | **0.000** | 80% |

With **no** continuation the control's breakout-vs-base *t* sits at **1.38** (p = 0.111) —
it does not fake an edge from a pretty shape (note the one-sample t vs zero is still 2.48,
exactly the drift trap the real tape exhibits). With a real planted drift it jumps to
**t = 8.87** (p = 0.000). The detector *can* find continuation when it exists — so the
real-tape null is a genuine null, not a blind detector.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The confirmed saucer breakout's forward return (**+1.51% at 20 days,
  +4.07% at 60**) **does not beat the every-bar base rate** (+1.14% / +3.31%): Welch
  *t* = 0.73 / 0.84, date-shuffle placebo *p* = 0.25 / 0.20. The one-sample *t* vs zero
  (2.97 / 4.52) is the **equity drift premium**, not a pattern signal. Survivorship would only
  flatter a real effect — there is none.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no excess over being long to harvest; 5 bps of cost turns
  an already-zero edge slightly negative. Nothing to size, so capacity and impact are moot.
- **"Accumulation signal"? — NOT SUPPORTED.** Across base-window {60, 90, 120} and fit
  R² {0.45, 0.55, 0.70} the breakout-vs-base *t* **never clears 2** (range −1.80 to +0.73);
  the "accumulation → markup regime change" leaves no measurable forward footprint. A rounding
  bottom is an after-the-fact *description* of a base that already formed, not a forward edge.
